drug_class: Bispecific antibody / Eye injection medication (anti-VEGF and anti-Ang-2 agent)
purpose: Faricimab-svoa is used to treat certain eye conditions that can cause vision loss, including wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD) and diabetic macular edema (DME). It helps protect your vision and in some cases may even improve it. Your doctor will use it to keep the disease from getting worse over time.
how_it_works: This medicine works by blocking two proteins in your eye — called VEGF and Ang-2 — that cause abnormal, leaky blood vessels to grow under your retina. By blocking both of these proteins at the same time, faricimab helps reduce swelling and fluid in the back of your eye. Think of it like patching two leaks at once, which helps keep your vision more stable.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include eye pain or discomfort, blurry vision after the injection, small spots or floaters in your vision, feeling like something is in your eye, and redness of the eye. These usually improve within a day or two after the injection.
warnings: Although rare, there is a small risk of serious eye infections (called endophthalmitis) or increased pressure inside your eye after the injection. Call your doctor right away if you have increasing eye pain, worsening redness, sensitivity to light, or sudden changes in vision. There is also a very small risk of a stroke or blood clot, so tell your doctor if you have had heart problems or a history of stroke.
typical_dosing: Faricimab is given as an injection directly into the eye by your eye doctor. For most patients, you will start with one injection every 4 weeks for the first few doses. After that, your doctor may be able to stretch the time between injections to every 8, 12, or even 16 weeks, depending on how your eye responds. Your doctor will decide the schedule that works best for you.
